Two measurements I produced were wrong and reached the options put to the owner before being re-measured. (1) A claim that four tables carry a parameter column; two do. Cause: one SQLite cursor reused for an inner query inside an outer iteration, which resets the outer cursor and silently truncates the loop, reporting a subset as the whole. The same bug had reported axes, item_axis_links and population_axis_map as absent from the schema when all three are live. (2) A count of AX- values using LIKE, which is case-insensitive for ASCII in SQLite, returning two source_locators rows that were 'tax-return' inside a Canada Revenue Agency URL. Both are recorded in references/project-standards.md with their mechanisms, because a derived document that the database does not support is CLAUDE.md 2(b)'s named failure and the mechanism is the reusable part.

bias_direction: My bias here is toward the ruling being tidier than it is. I want the owner's 'key on the canonical parameter' to be a clean carry-forward of a grain the schema already had, and I found real evidence for that reading -- the nullability pattern in source_value_extractions, the baseline's own GROUP BY, the index on (slug, parameter_canonical). The pressure that creates is to under-report what the ruling does not solve, and there is a specific thing it does not solve: parameter_canonical is unconstrained free text with no vocabulary, no CHECK, no registry and no writer, so a determination keyed on it can fragment across spellings of the same parameter. I mitigated by writing that counter-consideration into the RULE itself as a binding ACTION rather than a caveat in a scratch file, and by making the nullability problem explicit as an obligation on P1.2's writer. The second bias is procedural: having spent the session recording rulings, I am inclined to treat recording as completion. Nothing in this session executes anything. Not one line of the repair plan is implemented, the schema is untouched, and every ruling recorded remains a promise.
independent_reviewer_counterclaim: A reviewer could reasonably say this session moved a ruling from one document into another document and called it work. That charge has force. The strongest version: the preceding session diagnosed a severed pipeline, and the response to a severed pipeline has been two consecutive sessions of writing about it, producing a 1,434-line standards ledger and a 300-line plan against a judgment stage that still holds zero rows. The project's documented pathology is apparatus growing faster than the book, and prose about the apparatus is the cheapest apparatus of all. Three narrow defences. First, rule 0 makes recording a ruling on contact non-optional and the alternative is worse -- the ledger already records nine instances of paperwork being argued against live directives, and unrecorded rulings are how that happens. Second, the recording is not transcription: both 2026-08-26 rulings changed under measurement. The judgment-key ruling acquired a binding vocabulary obligation that nobody had noticed, and the register ruling turned out to be unexecutable as literally stated, because the matcher cannot express 'AX-' at all and an entry on the bare word 'axis' would flag the ordinary English that the governing DR explicitly protects. Both were discovered by reading the code rather than the intent. Third, the plan's ordering changed on evidence rather than on preference, including one claim of my own that had to be weakened: 'the population split must precede any cell write, categorically' stopped being categorical the moment the key it depended on was dropped, and I restated it downward rather than leaving the stronger version standing. What I cannot defend is the count: zero determinations, zero syntheses, zero rows anywhere the book is measured, for a second consecutive session.
